title: Sjögren's Disease With Primary Biliary Cholangitis Fulfilling the 2010 ACR/EULAR Classification Criteria for Rheumatoid Arthritis: A Case Report and Review of an Under-Recognized Overlap.
abstract: Sjögren's disease (SjD) and primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) are chronic autoimmune epithelitides that target exocrine glands and small intrahepatic bile ducts, respectively. Their coexistence is well described; less appreciated is a specific and avoidable failure mode. Because rheumatoid factor (RF) positivity, symmetric small-joint involvement and elevated acute-phase reactants are all common in SjD, patients with SjD-associated polyarthritis may reach the six-point threshold of the 2010 American College of Rheumatology/European League Against Rheumatism (ACR/EULAR) classification criteria for rheumatoid arthritis (RA); those criteria remain valid only if their mandatory exclusion clause is applied. We report a 49-year-old woman who carried a three-year diagnosis of RF-positive, anti-citrullinated peptide antibody (ACPA)-negative RA and had been treated with methotrexate and tofacitinib without ever developing radiographic erosions. Cholestatic liver injury during a course of amoxicillin-clavulanate led to the detection of anti-mitochondrial M2 antibodies and to a liver biopsy showing florid duct lesions with periductal granulomas, establishing stage 1 PBC. Directed questioning subsequently revealed a three-year history of previously unreported sicca symptoms. Anti-Sjögren's-syndrome-related antigen A autoantibodies (anti-Ro/SSA) were positive, the Schirmer test measured 1 mm bilaterally, and minor salivary gland biopsy demonstrated focal lymphocytic sialadenitis with a focus score of 2. These findings yielded a total of 7/9 points according to the 2016 ACR/EULAR classification criteria for SjD, with relevant exclusion criteria assessed and found to be absent. Immunosuppression was withdrawn, followed by sustained biochemical and articular improvement over 24 months after initiation of ursodeoxycholic acid and hydroxychloroquine. We review the epidemiology, shared immunopathogenesis, and therapeutic implications of the SjD-PBC overlap, and propose that, in an appropriate clinical context, a structured inquiry into sicca symptoms and consideration of anti-Ro/SSA testing may be useful in patients with ACPA-negative, RF-positive, non-erosive polyarthritis before escalation to biologic or targeted synthetic therapy.

title: Idiopathic Multicentric Castleman Disease Mimicking Sepsis and Autoimmune Disease in a Caribbean Patient.
abstract: Idiopathic multicentric Castleman disease (iMCD) is a rare cytokine-driven lymphoproliferative disorder characterised by systemic inflammation, generalised lymphadenopathy, and multiorgan involvement. Its clinical presentation may closely mimic sepsis, autoimmune disease, and other inflammatory disorders, creating a significant diagnostic challenge, particularly in resource-limited settings. We describe a 73-year-old Caribbean woman who presented with approximately one month of fever, progressive unintentional weight loss, profound fatigue, bilateral lower-limb oedema, and cutaneous hyperpigmentation. She was initially evaluated for sepsis and treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics for one week; however, microbiological investigations were negative, and there was no significant clinical improvement. Laboratory investigations demonstrated marked systemic inflammation, anaemia, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, and hypoalbuminaemia. Computed tomography revealed generalised lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly, with additional thoracic findings including interstitial lung changes and small pleural and pericardial effusions. Autoimmune serology showed isolated ANA positivity, with dsDNA, ENA subtypes, rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP, and ANCA all negative - not meeting criteria for an alternative connective tissue disease. Excisional lymph node biopsy demonstrated atrophic germinal centres, expanded mantle zones, and polyclonal plasmacytosis, while testing for human herpesvirus-8 and immunoglobulin G4 was negative, confirming iMCD. A concurrent breast mass identified on imaging was biopsied and showed features in keeping with iMCD rather than malignancy. Treatment included corticosteroids, hydroxychloroquine, and azathioprine, with supportive therapy. During a severe inflammatory flare six weeks after admission, tocilizumab produced transient clinical and biochemical improvement, but she developed pruritus, angioedema, and shortness of breath during infusion; thus, ongoing biologic therapy was not continued. She has since been followed for approximately 19 months with a relapsing course managed through sequential steroid-sparing agents, with improved fatigue, weight gain, and improved quality of life despite residual cutaneous changes. This case highlights the importance of considering iMCD in patients with persistent systemic inflammation, generalised lymphadenopathy, cytopenias, and a negative infectious work-up and non-lupus-specific autoimmune profile, and illustrates the practical challenges of sustaining guideline-directed biologic therapy in a resource-limited Caribbean setting.
